What is the belief of atheists regarding the explanation of everything through science? Is there a possibility of something beyond explanation according to atheists? Atheists, by definition, generally subscribe to the idea that scientific inquiry, particularly empirical investigation and the scientific method, is the best way to understand the natural world. They don't necessarily believe that science provides all the answers, since science is a continuous process of refinement and discovery. However, they are usually skeptical of explanations that fall outside the realm of scientific understanding, and favor explanations that are supported by evidence and rigorous testing. They don't rule out the possibility of presently unknown phenomena or new scientific discoveries, but they don't assume them either. To them, all explanations can be subject to scientific scrutiny. If it can't be tested, then it's likely outside the realm of science. Therefore, by definition, any belief in something beyond scientific explanation would not be considered within the scope of atheism's core tenets.

Atheists, isn't your Darwinian theory a little far-fetched when you think about it? The theory states that all living things have a common ancestor. An elephant and a mosquito share a common ancestor? Really? Well, sure. That's what the theory predicts. Humans and mushrooms share a common ancestor. That's not to say that elephants and mosquitos didn't have many ancestors that were just elephants and mosquitos, respectively. In fact, that's basically the entire point. It's not that the modern elephant and the modern mosquito are closely related. It's that if you keep going further and further back, you'll eventually find a point where the lineages, or the branches of the family tree, converge. That's the 'common ancestor' idea. It's not so much 'far-fetched' as it is 'counter-intuitive.' When you're used to thinking about animals in the modern day, it's hard to jump back hundreds of millions or billions of years. It's probably one of the biggest problems in teaching evolutionary biology. People struggle to think about a shared past. People also get very hung up on the word 'theory'. By scientific standards, a 'theory' isn't just a guess. It's the scientific explanation for some observation, which is built on a large body of evidence, and has stood up to rigorous testing. Evolution, as a theory, has been tested and retested countless times. And the evidence keeps piling up. The theory of evolution is one of the most robust theories in all of science, supported by evidence from genetics, paleontology, comparative anatomy, and biogeography, among many other disciplines. It's not all that different than the Theory of Gravity, or the Big Bang Theory. So no, it's not far-fetched. It's just that trying to picture the relationships between living things, going back that far in time, can be a bit of a mental puzzle without the proper education.

Do they still teach the myth about Columbus being the first European to reach the Americas in US schools? Unfortunately, it seems like that's still a common lesson, even though it's demonstrably false. The Vikings were here centuries before Columbus. They even established a short-lived settlement in Newfoundland. But the story of Columbus is the one that stuck, and it's taught as fact to millions of schoolchildren every year. ABOVE SOURCE: What do kids learn in US schools about Columbus and the Americas? - The Washington Post It’s not just a simple factual error, either. The Columbus narrative glosses over or outright ignores the devastating consequences of European contact on the indigenous populations of the Americas. Diseases, enslavement, and warfare decimated entire civilizations. It's a pretty problematic thing to present as some sort of heroic tale. The fact that so many people still believe it, despite readily available information, is a problem, especially considering the critical thinking skills that children are supposed to be learning in school. There are a lot of reasons why this historical inaccuracy persists, including historical inertia, political biases, and issues of cultural representation. It's going to take a conscious effort to change this narrative. And a lot of people are already working on doing just that. It’s not just about correcting the historical record, however. It’s about teaching kids to think critically, question their sources, and understand the complexities of history.

Is it considered rude to be served on paper plates and plastic utensils at a dinner party? Depends on the dinner party, right? If it's some stuffy black-tie affair or a formal holiday gathering at someone's mansion, then yeah, it probably would be considered a bit uncouth. You'd likely be expecting fine china, silverware, and maybe even a sommelier to go along with it. But if it's a casual get-together—a backyard barbecue, a game night, or maybe just a potluck with friends—then it's perfectly acceptable, and arguably the more pragmatic choice. Let's face it: nobody wants to spend half the next day washing dishes after a fun evening. The emphasis is on the company, not the accoutrements. Plastic and paper are often the way to go for low-key affairs. They're easy to clean up, they're less of a hassle, and they can actually be pretty stylish these days. You can get some pretty classy-looking paper plates, and good quality plastic utensils can be a huge step up from the flimsy stuff that bends every time you try to cut your steak. Of course, you'd never use them at a wedding's plated meal or a fancy gala.

Are atheists truly correct if everything has to have a creator? The Earth can't come out of nothingness. It had to be created by something. But, if everything has a creator, then what created that creator? And what created that creator’s creator? It’s turtles all the way down. You very quickly get into an infinite regression, and you really haven’t solved anything. You just re-labeled the problem and made it more complicated. This is an old philosophical argument that goes back centuries. I'm not particularly religious myself, but I’ve always felt that the simple answer is that the universe just *is*. It doesn’t need to have a creator. It never started; it never stopped. It just *was*. The universe is a closed system of matter and energy that is conserved. Energy can't be created or destroyed. It just gets turned into different forms. And so yeah, I agree that the Earth did not come out of nothingness, but neither did the universe.

I have responded to a fare number of Christian trolls on here as a Christian myself, so this is an honest question. Regardless of which theistic religion, would there be anything that could convince you of the existence of a god(s)? If so, wouldn’t that make you more agnostic that truly atheist? (I believe the wisest amongst us are the agnostics) This is a thought-provoking query, one I'm happy to tackle, though it's a complex one that defies a simple “yes” or “no” answer. As an engineer, I'm trained to deal in facts and evidence. I'm skeptical by nature, which means I require tangible proof before accepting any claim, especially one as extraordinary as the existence of a deity. So, to answer your question directly, yes, there are potential scenarios that could sway my perspective. If I were presented with undeniable, empirical evidence – something that could be replicated and verified by the scientific community – that a god or gods exist, I would have no choice but to acknowledge it. I'm thinking of something along the lines of a phenomenon that demonstrably violates the laws of physics as we understand them, and where the only logical explanation is intervention from a supernatural force. Alternatively, let's say that every major religion on the planet was to produce a miracle, simultaneously, that defied current scientific understanding. If that happened I would have to at least acknowledge the possibility of divine intervention. But, let's be honest, I'm not holding my breath.That said, it's true that I would then fall squarely into the agnostic camp. Becoming convinced of a god's existence wouldn't magically transform me into a devout believer. The core of my skepticism would remain, tempered by the acceptance of new information. I still would have an awful lot of questions regarding the nature of this god, its motivations, the meaning of existing, and why it waited so long to present this undeniable evidence to the rest of us. So, while the evidence might tilt me away from atheism, it wouldn’t immediately align me with any specific religion, as that would require additional, circumstantial evidence. I'd continue to analyze the evidence, weigh the arguments, and refine my understanding. The wisest among us, as you astutely observe, are indeed the agnostics. It's the most honest and intellectually sound position, in my opinion. It acknowledges the limits of our knowledge and the potential for the unknown.

So why are pilots who have been flying for years all saying they know the earth is flat? You're going to have to clarify what you mean by "all." There are a lot of people who have claimed to be pilots for years, and who are definitely saying the Earth is flat. But they're usually not *real* pilots. The ones who *are* real pilots, with commercial or military flight hours under their belt, virtually all agree the Earth is a sphere (or more technically, an oblate spheroid). Do I need to show you the photos and videos of the Earth from space? Do I need to explain how GPS satellites, which are critical for navigation, will only work if you believe the Earth is a sphere? I could pull up some flight paths and show you how planes fly around the globe -- as you can do yourself just by using one of the flight tracking websites. But I think you get my point. The number of real pilots who hold the view that the Earth is flat is vanishingly small, if it exists at all. You can go ahead and look for them if you want, but I'm not going to bother. I'm going to assume you're talking about the other group of people. So why *are* these people saying the Earth is flat? Well, first off, what's with the whole "they" and "them" business? Who exactly *are* "they"? And if you really want to know why "they" believe what they do, then you should simply go ask "them." You're going to have to wade through a lot of bizarre opinions, but at least you can get it from the horse's mouth, instead of me trying to summarize it all. But, alright, I'll give it a go and try to explain some of the most common arguments I've seen. A lot of these folks seem to think it's all one big conspiracy. The government, NASA, and every scientist, educator, or pilot are all in on it to keep the truth from the world. Why? That part is, of course, usually nebulous at best. Sometimes they'll vaguely gesture towards a "New World Order" who want to control us all, or they'll suggest some kind of financial gain for the "lie." But usually, there's not much in the way of supporting evidence.

Some people say Jesus didn’t resurrect but was resuscitated by Joseph of Arimathea, after which he lived secretly in other parts of the world till the age of eighty. If true, why didn’t the apostles know about this and allegedly died as martyrs? That's quite the conspiracy theory, isn't it? This notion that Jesus merely *appeared* to die, then made a miraculous recovery – only to vanish incognito throughout the late Roman Empire, is one hell of a plot twist. It conveniently explains away the problem of the crucifixion, the resurrection narrative, and the martyrdoms of the early apostles, but it frankly necessitates more leaps of faith than the traditional story. Consider the logistical nightmare: Joseph of Arimathea has to be a master medic, skilled enough to revive someone apparently dead from crucifixion with no training, and then keep that secret between them. Further complexities arise from how this secret recovery aligns with the stories of the disciples experiencing the resurrected Christ. And what about the claim that the apostles died as martyrs? If they knew Jesus was alive all along, wouldn't they be in on the secret? Or, did they feign their own deaths for some convoluted reason? It simply doesn’t hold water when you begin to dissect the story. The whole thing reeks of historical revisionism cooked up by those seeking to undermine the foundational beliefs of Christianity. It’s a seductive thought, I'll give you that. It’s the equivalent of a good sci-fi story, full of mystery and speculation, but has zero basis in reality.

👋 Hello. Although I have many reservations about the New Testament, I wonder why so many people put pen to paper about the life of Jesus. What inspired them to write about his life. Surely there is a 'Kernel ' of truth contained within them? It's a fair question, I suppose. What spurred those early scribes to detail the events surrounding Jesus? And, conceding my own skepticism, is there a scintilla of veracity hidden within the Gospels, buried beneath layers of interpretation and retelling? The motivations behind early religious texts are often complex, influenced by a mix of personal conviction, communal needs, and, yes, perhaps a kernel of historical fact. Considering the scant attention given to many other figures of that era, the enduring focus on Jesus is striking. Why him? What made his story so compelling, so worth documenting and propagating, that it survived the passage of time and continues to resonate with billions? The answer likely involves a potent mix of factors: Charisma, the power of a compelling message, and the undeniable human inclination to seek meaning and purpose. It's tempting to dismiss it all as pure fabrication; a convenient narrative crafted to suit the needs of a burgeoning faith. The skeptical side of me certainly leans in that direction. However, it's equally plausible that the story, as amplified over the years, retains a fragile core of authenticity. Perhaps eyewitness accounts, however imperfect, formed the basis for initial writings. Regardless, that core has since mutated over time. What survives today is a blend of oral tradition, written accounts, theological interpretations, and the inherent human drive to mythologize and elevate key figures. The challenge, for any critical observer, is to separate the wheat from the chaff, to discern what might be factual from what clearly isn't. A daunting task, indeed.

Maybe a biology teach in a public school can’t teach the truth about the existence of life. But can she point out the fallacies of evolution without speaking about creationism? Is that unconstitutional? That's a tricky proposition, wading into the murky waters of what a public school teacher can and can't do. On one hand, there's the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment, which generally prevents the government from establishing or endorsing a religion. That has been interpreted by the courts as precluding teachers from proselytizing or promoting any particular religious view, including creationism. On the other hand, there's academic freedom, which allows teachers to discuss a wide range of scientific theories, even if those theories are controversial or challenge prevailing beliefs. The real kicker comes when you try to separate honest scientific discourse from advocacy for a particular religious viewpoint. Could a biology teacher critique the theory of evolution, pointing out flaws, inconsistencies, or areas of ongoing debate, without simultaneously advocating for intelligent design or creationism? Absolutely. Science thrives on skepticism and questioning established ideas. The scientific method itself is built around challenging assumptions and searching for evidence that might overturn existing theories. A teacher could present the "problems" with evolution – gaps in the fossil record, incomplete explanations for complex biological systems, ongoing challenges to current models – as examples of ongoing scientific inquiry. The teacher is not stating as fact things are happening. This is what is in the scientific research.

WHEN does the real future of radical improvement like safe flying cars for the masses, holographic movies, massive building structures like seen in Judge Dredd etc actually start? Are we trapped in the present nightmare of potholes, jammed roads etc? A question that has certainly crossed the mind of every sci-fi enthusiast, right? The allure of a future unfettered by the mundane realities that bog us down – the traffic snarls, the cracked pavements, the constant delays. Yet, here we are, seemingly tethered to the here and now. While the Jetsons promised a world of airborne vehicles and automated everything, we’re often left grappling with the daily grind. But let's not succumb to cynicism and declare our dreams utterly unattainable. Progress, while not always linear, is nonetheless relentless. Perhaps those flying cars, or at least some semblance of them, are closer than we think. The technology exists, the challenges are surmountable, and the societal benefits are undeniable. Similarly, advancements in virtual and augmented realities are rapidly blurring those lines between the physical and digital worlds. So, can we expect a sudden shift, a radical leap into the future that's been depicted in the movies? Probably not. But slow incremental steps? Quite possibly, and that in itself is a form of progress.

Could Kamala Harris beat Donald Trump? Yes. And Trump could beat Harris. The 2024 election will be no different than the last few. Polling will be all over the place, but the actual election results will be remarkably close. The campaigns will each get out their voters, and the swing states will decide it. There are just two candidates. One of them is going to win. It’s not even that the candidate with better policies, or more charisma, or better hair will beat the other one. Each candidate is just as likely to win. It’s mostly the luck of the draw, with a bit of strategic maneuvering from the campaigns. Remember, too, that voters’ minds can change. Anything can happen between now and election day. I'm trying to avoid making any predictions at this point, since I'm not going to have any special insight.

What is the probability that a satellite the size of the moon, would orbit just the right distance from a planet the size of the earth, that from the planet, it appears the same size as a star the size of the sun, at its distance from that planet? It's a fun thought experiment, isn't it? Let's break down the problem a bit. Clearly, the "just the right distance" has to do with the gravitational forces involved, but there are many, many possible orbital radii that would be stable for a satellite. But the requirement that the moon-sized satellite appears the same size as the sun-sized star, viewed from the Earth-sized planet, greatly narrows down the range of possible distances. Since we're talking about angular size, we're really only concerned with the ratio of the objects' sizes to their distances. The Sun is roughly 400 times larger than the Moon, but it's also roughly 400 times farther away. Thus, they appear to be roughly the same size in the sky. So the "just the right distance" boils down to any distance where that ratio holds. And what is the probability of this happening? Well, it's not zero, given that it has *already* happened. We live on a planet where this occurs, so we already have one data point. From that, we can work backwards to get the odds. It's not a question of *if* such a configuration is possible. It is. The laws of physics allow for it. The real questions are: How rare is it? And how much does it matter? For the purpose of this analysis, let's go with the known values: the ratio of the sizes and the distances. We know the Sun is roughly 400 times wider than the Moon and 400 times farther from Earth. That means the Moon distance to our planet has a range of possibilities given that the Sun emits the same amount of energy relative to the Moon's size. This is quite a narrow range, but still achievable. Considering how many planets, moons, and stars there are in the universe, the odds of this scenario happening somewhere are reasonably high. Probably not as inevitable as the formation of life itself, but certainly something we should expect to find quite a bit of. And how much does it matter? Well, it matters a good bit to us. The alignment is the source of solar eclipses, one of the most beautiful astronomical events visible to the naked eye, thus allowing us to study the sun's corona. I'd say we have a pretty good reason to count ourselves fortunate.

If the weight of a body in water is 12N and weight of liquid displaced by the body is 8N, then what is the weights of that object in air? The buoyant force acting on an object is equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by the object. In this scenario, we are told that the weight of the liquid displaced by the body is 8N. Therefore, the buoyant force acting on the object is 8N. The weight of an object in a fluid is equal to its weight in air minus the buoyant force. So, if the weight of the object in water is 12N, and the buoyant force is 8N, then the weight of the object in air will be the sum of the weight in water and the buoyant force. Weight in air = Weight in water + Buoyant force. Weight in air = 12N + 8N. Weight in air = 20N That’s the answer. What prompted this question? Were you doing some sort of homework problem, or just genuinely curious? Is it from a textbook somewhere? Or some physics problem set? Either way, it's a pretty straightforward application of Archimedes’ principle. I've always thought it's such a delightfully counterintuitive concept. That something can be so buoyant that it pushes something else away, like a body floating in water displacing the water around it. Funny old world, sometimes. You can feel the force of buoyancy when you're in a swimming pool. It makes you feel lighter. It’s a great thing, for sure, except when you're trying to dive down to the bottom of a pool to retrieve a dropped item, and you have to overcome the buoyancy to do so. I’m sometimes amazed that we can calculate these forces to a high degree of accuracy, or that we understand the principles behind them at all.

Why are millenial and gen Z women so much likelier to wait until their 30s to settle down and are far more sleighted to want to sleep around with tens of people before earnestly looking for a partner? No shame, no blame. Just curious. There are countless possible contributing factors behind this evolving trend, and I am not in the business of doling out definitive answers. Societal norms have undergone a seismic shift, and the expectation of early marriage and rapid childbearing has dissipated significantly. Women now have far greater opportunities to pursue education, build careers, and establish financial independence prior to settling down. The allure of "settling down" has also changed. It's no longer viewed as a necessity in the same way as it once was. Also, the availability of reliable contraception plays its role, affording greater control over reproductive choices. The stigma surrounding premarital sex, too, has noticeably lessened. Young women are increasingly empowered to define their own paths, irrespective of traditional expectations. Furthermore, there's the undeniable influence of social media, which has altered every facet of our lives, including courtship rituals. The emphasis on personal freedom and self-discovery, coupled with a broader acceptance of diverse lifestyles, undoubtedly plays a huge role. It's a complex interplay of cultural, economic, and personal factors that varies across individuals. And it’s worth mentioning, as the question alludes to, but does not explicitly outline, that this is not a phenomenon exclusive to women, and similar shifts are readily apparent in young men as well.

Scientists dabble and meddle in the genome with the intent to make life better, but are they really, intentionally or unintentionally, redefining or redesigning life? If so, how? I'm an aerospace engineer, not a biologist, but I can certainly offer some thoughts based on my own understanding of science and technology. The short answer is, yes, both intentionally and unintentionally. It's an undeniable aspect of what's happening right now. Gene editing, with tools like CRISPR-Cas9, allows scientists to precisely alter the genetic code of organisms. This has opened up possibilities for treating genetic diseases, developing disease-resistant crops, and even enhancing human traits. And of course, that's just what we know about through public sources. But you can't just change everything to be perfect though. Everything has tradeoffs, and the changes that would be made to life would come with some unintended consequences that would need to be further studied. It's like when a software engineer makes a change to a code, something that was working fine stops working. But that makes the code "better" since it gets rid of the original issues of the code. And eventually, everything is better in the end. We hope.

Have you ever met an intelligent creationist? Yes, I have. It's actually somewhat difficult to define what is meant by "creationism." The word covers quite a range of beliefs, and the people who hold those beliefs, even within a narrow slice of creationism, are generally very intelligent. For example, there are people who believe in a literal interpretation of the Bible, and thus don't accept the findings of modern scientific disciplines like biology, geology, and astrophysics. These individuals often feel that scientific theories like evolution are inherently in conflict with their religious beliefs. However, it's also possible to be a theistic evolutionist, believing in the broad strokes of evolution while also believing that a divine power played a role in the process. These people, even if they don't accept all the particulars of science, are often just as well-versed in current scientific knowledge as anybody else. I'm reminded here of a joke regarding my own profession, aerospace engineering, which is that the purpose of our discipline is to give an excuse to make more expensive art. In any case, to answer the question, yes. I have known intelligent creationists.

How many hours do you need to exercise to lose weight? There’s no one-size-fits-all answer to that question, as it hinges on a confluence of factors. It's a nuanced interplay of metabolic rate, dietary habits, and the inherent physical makeup of the individual. To be blunt, you can't outrun a bad diet. You could spend hours slogging away at the gym, but if your caloric intake consistently outstrips your expenditure, you're fighting an uphill battle. Think of it like a budget. If you're relentlessly spending more than you earn, you will inevitably go broke. Exercise is undoubtedly a crucial piece of the puzzle, a cornerstone of overall well-being, but it’s only one component. In fact, there's some debate on the exact numbers. Numerous sources proffer varying recommendations, often citing anywhere from 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise per week, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous-intensity activity. But these are just guidelines.

Are there any fossil remains of the fish that decided to walk onto land, thus becoming a man? No. But the fossil record is pretty extensive, and if such a thing were to have happened, we would most certainly have a good collection of fossilized remains. The transition from fish to land-dwelling creatures was not a sudden leap, but a gradual process. We can trace the lineage through a series of intermediate forms, each with a mix of aquatic and terrestrial traits. The best example of this is *Tiktaalik roseae*, a fish that lived around 375 million years ago. It had scales and gills like a fish, but also had sturdy fins that could support its weight on land, and a neck and ribs, features not typically found in a fish. It's a textbook example of a transitional fossil that shows how life can evolve in such amazing new forms. Another key fossil is *Panderichthys*, which predates *Tiktaalik* by around 10 million years. While it had more fish-like traits than *Tiktaalik*, it, too, shows adaptations hinting at life outside the water. Then there is *Acanthostega*, a creature that lived about 10 million years after *Tiktaalik*, that shows four limbs and the first steps of walking on land. The point is, the change from fish to land was gradual, and it wasn't a case of one fish suddenly deciding to get out of the water and turn into a human. Instead, it involved many generations of creatures adapting to increasingly terrestrial environments.

Is Terrence Howard right that 1 + 0 = 1 and 1 x 1 = 2? No. In the simplest terms, the answer is emphatically no. Perhaps Terrence Howard has a different understanding of math than the rest of us. Or perhaps he's attempting to pull a fast one on all of us. In either case, just because someone is an actor (or a physicist) doesn't mean they're an expert in all fields. It’s a shame that some people with an audience will say things like this. This is not to say that you shouldn’t listen to people who are experts in a particular field. I enjoy watching videos from people who are experts on, for example, the current state of space exploration, since that's one of their areas of expertise. But you should be skeptical of anything they say that strays outside of their particular field of expertise. Even if they are generally intelligent and well-informed people. It's not that they're intentionally making stuff up. It's just that people are often overconfident in their own knowledge. Even when they don’t know what they're talking about. To get an idea of how smart some people are, consider that the average IQ, by definition, is 100. The vast majority of people fall somewhere between 85 and 115. And then there's people like Albert Einstein whose IQ was likely in the range of 160. What's important to keep in mind is that any given person is likely an expert in only a few subjects. So if you encounter those people, you should be aware of their limitations.

Why do people seem to think gun control laws matter when in reality if I want to obtain a gun and the government thought it could stop me, I'd just obtain a gun through illegal means? It's a fair question, and one that's often debated. The crux of the argument boils down to the effectiveness of laws in deterring those with ill intentions. If someone is determined to acquire a firearm for unlawful purposes, the prevailing sentiment is that they'll find a way, regardless of legal constraints. That sentiment certainly resonates with a certain segment of the population. This perspective often underscores the futility of such regulations, as criminals, by definition, operate outside the bounds of the law. They aren't known for their adherence to societal norms, let alone legislative edicts. This line of reasoning assumes that the laws are primarily followed by law-abiding citizens, while those inclined towards criminal activity will simply resort to alternative and illicit methods of procurement. The logic suggests that gun control measures primarily impact the ability of the average citizen to legally own a firearm, while doing little to impede a criminal's access to weaponry.

Do atheists actually believe they are monkeys? Do they have an urge to climb trees? Is it sad to only believe in one’s self? No to all of the above. Atheists don't believe they are monkeys, they don't have any inclination to climb trees, and believing in yourself is quite different from atheism. I think someone must have had a rather simplistic view of what atheism is. It's simply a lack of belief in a god or gods. Absolutely nothing more. It’s a single answer to one question, but not a whole worldview. It could be that atheists believe in other things and have other ways of explaining the world.If you want to build up a whole worldview, that's generally called philosophy. You can of course be atheist and make up your own specific philosophy, but that’s not required, and that’s not what atheism itself is. Atheists can be consequentialists, or deontologists, or a whole mix of different philosophies. The reverse is also true. You can also have a philosophy and then not believe there’s a god. But you don't have to.Furthermore, not believing in a god isn't necessarily the only defining characteristic of an atheist. The only thing all atheists have in common is just that they don't believe in a god, but they can vary on many other things. Some atheists consider themselves spiritual. Some are very active in their atheism, while others just don't care about religion. It just depends on what is important to the individual. It really comes down to the person.

Who was the first ancestor of ours who walked on four legs? There are a lot of organisms out there that walked on four legs. And the answer to this particular question is going to depend on how you define "ancestor" and "ours". But for the sake of this discussion, I’m going to assume that you mean the ancestor who's most directly in the lineage that led up to modern humans. To put it another way, I’m going to assume you're asking about the last common ancestor of modern humans and modern chimpanzees. This creature, let's face it, is something that has long eluded the scientific community. Paleontologists, evolutionary biologists, and geneticists have been trying to unravel this mystery for decades, sifting through fossil records and comparing DNA sequences. The fossil record, unfortunately, is riddled with gaps. Bones, after all, are a bit fragile, particularly after they've been sitting in the ground for millions of years. Finding a complete skeleton is like finding the Holy Grail of paleoanthropology. The evidence we do have suggests that this last common ancestor, or at least creatures very similar to it, probably existed somewhere between 6 and 8 million years ago. It would have been a primate, of course, and most likely lived in Africa, where many of our earliest hominin fossils have been found. It probably possessed a combination of features. It likely retained some arboreal (tree dwelling) traits from its earlier primate cousins, but also started to show signs of the evolution of bipedalism (walking on two legs). The early hominins had to have the right mix for their own survival, and the evolution of our own.

Some worry that the United States is in an unusually anti-intellectual period right now. Is this really the case? Haven't societies always been composed mostly of people who are rather unthinking and just want "bread and circuses"? It's a fair question to pose. Human history is littered with examples of vast populations preoccupied with immediate needs and diversions. The masses, throughout history, have often prioritized survival and entertainment over rigorous intellectual pursuits. Consider the Roman Empire, with its "bread and circuses" designed to pacify the populace. Or the countless other civilizations where the vast majority of people simply focused on day-to-day existence, largely unconcerned with abstract thought or philosophical debates. ABOVE SOURCE: The Roman Empire | Wikipedia Even in societies we might consider intellectual hotbeds, like ancient Greece, the ratio of those engaged in complex thought to those absorbed in daily labor or leisure was likely quite skewed. Think of the great philosophers and scientists of ancient Greece, like Plato and Aristotle. They were intellectual giants, but that tiny minority were by definition, a minority. It's not as if everyone else was sitting around philosophizing all day alongside them. Indeed, the very structure of most earlier societies, with their rigid hierarchies, limited access to education, and the ever-present struggle for basic resources, did not lend themselves to widespread intellectualism. One could argue that the concept of a society *primarily* devoted to intellectual pursuits is a relatively modern one, perhaps only emerging in the last few centuries.

Question for atheists- how do you feel about Christians talking about their faith with you if they are nice about it (ie not screaming that you are going to Hell)? Do Christians in this manner bother you? I hope my question makes sense. I'm an atheist because I don't believe in the existence of any gods. But that's a personal choice, and it doesn't mean I have any problem with other people having religious beliefs. If somebody wants to talk about their faith, I'm fine with that, as long as they're not being pushy or condescending. Frankly, I'd be more bothered by somebody who demanded I believe or act a certain way, than somebody who was simply expressing their own beliefs. If they're genuinely interested in a dialogue, I'm all for it. I'm even open to changing my mind, if they could somehow come up with compelling evidence to support their claims. But if they start making threats or assuming they know better, then yeah, I'll probably tune them out. And I certainly won't be joining their church. I don’t have an issue with Christians, or people of any faith, just as long as they keep the conversation on the level. I am a huge fan of the First Amendment, which guarantees people their right to practice their chosen religion. Live and let live, as the saying goes.

You say that Darwin proved we are all animals, but animals rarely practice birthcontrol, then why you do? That's a fair question, but it's a bit of a non-starter. The entire concept of birth control is a relatively recent invention, a blip in the vast timeline of evolution. To expect animals to suddenly start employing it doesn't align with how natural selection operates. Humans, on the other hand, have the unique capacity to understand the mechanics of reproduction and to act upon that understanding—we can make informed choices. We're not just driven by instinct, although that's certainly still a significant factor. But as humans, we have the ability to think about the consequences of our actions, to plan for the future. So yeah, we practice birth control. We have the ability and capacity to make the choice. Other animals? They either don’t, or can’t. It really is as simple as that.

Is it better to fly two long haul flights (say 10 hours each) instead of one ultra-long haul flight (about 18-19 hours)? It appears that the answer depends greatly on personal preference and the specific circumstances surrounding the flights. A traveler has to weigh several factors. A shorter flight might be preferable since it generally would involve less time spent cooped up in a metal tube, but they also get you into a new airport and terminal for a layover. When you are in the air for a longer time, this might allow you to get more sleep, watch three or four movies, and get through most of the in-flight magazine. But it also means more time with the cramped airplane lavatory and a greater degree of exposure to the recycled air of the cabin. Then there is the consideration of any layover, which can offer the opportunity to stretch your legs, get some fresh air, and maybe even grab a decent meal. However, layovers also introduce potential for delays, lost luggage, and the added burden of navigating a new airport. Also, keep in mind that the longer the flight, the greater the probability that something will go wrong. And then of course, you have to consider any travel cost. If the shorter flights involve a layover, they might actually cost less, or it might be more costly. It's all down to the individual traveler's priorities and tolerance levels.

As a native-English-language-speaker, is there ever situation in which you actually should not speak perfectly accurate English as defined by most academically approved English grammar and vocabulary books? Yes, absolutely. There are plenty of instances where a more, shall we say, *flexible* approach to the Queen’s English is not only acceptable but downright preferable. Think of it like this: you wouldn’t exactly wear a tuxedo to go mudding in your pickup truck, would you? The tools have to match the job.Consider a casual conversation with friends. Do you really need to trot out the full formal syntax and sophisticated vocabulary for a friendly chat about the ballgame or the latest blockbuster? No way. You’d sound like a pompous windbag, and the whole vibe would be ruined. It's about connecting, not about showing off your linguistic prowess.Or, what about communicating with people who aren’t native English speakers? Sometimes, simplifying your language can be a lot more effective than sticking to every single rule. It’s about ensuring they *understand* you, not making them admire your grammar. That’s the important bit.Then there’s creative writing. Authors intentionally bend the rules all the time to create character, mood, and voice. Slang. Dialect. Broken grammar. They’re all tools in a writer’s arsenal. And many famous writers have made their careers doing just that.In short, while it's important to know the rules, it's equally important to know when to break them. Communication is the key. And sometimes, a little imperfection goes a long way.

Should creationism be taught in public schools as an alternative to evolution, given its religious roots, or does doing so infringe upon the separation of church and state? No, the separation of church and state prohibits the teaching of creationism in a public school science class. The Supreme Court has ruled on this. Public schools should be teaching science, and evolution is a scientific theory. Creationism is a religious belief, not a scientific one. Should religious texts be taught in a comparative religion class? Sure, as long as other religious texts are taught there as well. But it’s not a science. The primary goal of a science class is to teach students the scientific method, evidence-based reasoning, and how the natural world works. Public education is not about indoctrination. It's about equipping students with the critical thinking skills necessary to evaluate information, make informed decisions, and understand the world around them. This includes learning about various scientific theories, such as evolution, and the evidence supporting them. Trying to sneak other ideas into this is not the way to make an informed populace. A teacher doesn’t have to agree with their students. They mostly just have to let the students come to their own conclusions. The teacher must be able to stick to teaching the material at hand, and the students have to get their own grades. If the teacher can't do those two things, or the students can't do those two things, then something's not working. I'm all for allowing students to explore different worldviews, but it needs to be done in a way that doesn’t turn the classroom into a battleground for religious or political ideologies.

Is music at best better than food? That's a real head-scratcher, isn't it? The eternal question of art versus sustenance. I'm inclined to say no, and here’s the reasoning behind my take on things. Humans need to eat; it's a fundamental requirement for survival. Without food, we perish. Music, on the other hand, is a luxury, a pleasure. It enhances life, to be sure, but it's not essential for it. You can live a perfectly healthy life without ever hearing a note of music. You can do the hard work of surviving without even being able to enjoy music. One can't say the same about food. You need it to even function. Sure, music might stir the soul and bring joy in ways that food doesn't always manage. You can enjoy a symphony of your favorite sounds, but at the end of the day, you’re still going to need to eat. Now, if we're talking about the joy music brings, or maybe a sense of community, or the way music taps into emotions, yes, music can be better. But in a survival scenario, food wins. It's the foundation upon which everything else is built. So, while music might elevate the human experience, it's not as fundamental as a solid meal.

What movies were marketed in a very misleading way, making the audience expect something different from what was presented? This is a fun topic, and I’m sure all of us, at one time or another, have felt hoodwinked by a trailer or a poster promising something the movie itself failed to deliver. Let's kick things off with some personal experience. I vividly recall seeing the trailer for "Alien 3" back in the day. It presented a gritty, claustrophobic return to the horror of the original, a real back-to-basics approach. I was anticipating a tension-filled, suspenseful thrill ride. Instead, what I got was…well, let’s just say a lot less satisfying. The film felt disjointed, with a narrative that didn't quite gel together, and a general lack of the dread the trailer had promised. It was like they took all the best parts of the marketing campaign and then completely bungled the execution. On the other hand, the marketing for the original "Alien" masterfully did its job, keeping a large part of the plot secret, allowing for a slow burn that led to a massive pay-off once the chestburster scene happened. That's the ideal scenario, really. But "Alien 3"…well, they really missed the mark. Then, there's the well-documented case of "Suicide Squad." The trailers were jam-packed with flashy imagery, a killer soundtrack, and a distinct sense of fun, promising a dark yet humorous romp through the DC universe. The actual film, however… felt like a chopped-up mess, and what fun it had was lost between massive studio interference and a lack of direction. The characters, which promised to be compelling, memorable anti-heroes, were, frankly, a bit flat. The end result was an incoherent narrative, even if the soundtrack was still great. Another film that comes to mind is "Drive," the 2011 Ryan Gosling movie directed by Nicolas Winding Refn. The trailers led many viewers to expect a fast-paced, action-packed car chase film that felt like a spiritual successor to "Fast and Furious". What the audience got instead was a slow-burning, stylish crime drama with an emphasis on character development and the mood of Los Angeles. It's a genuinely great film, but some found it a disappointment solely because of the misleading marketing.

What evidence supports the theory of natural selection and evolution as the origin of life on Earth, according to Charles Darwin? Darwin's body of work amassed volumes of observations, experiments, and inferences backing his framework for natural selection. He meticulously documented the variations within species, the struggles for existence, and the concept of "survival of the fittest." His core argument rested on several key pieces of evidence. First, there's the remarkable fossil record, showcasing a progression of life forms through time, with simpler organisms appearing earlier and more complex ones emerging later. This paleontological evidence illustrated a branching pattern of evolution, with common ancestors giving rise to diverse lineages. Then, there is the geographical distribution of plants and animals. Darwin observed that species on different continents, though sharing similar environments, often displayed distinct characteristics, implying adaptation to local conditions. Furthermore, comparative anatomy provided compelling insights. The structural similarities of seemingly dissimilar animals, such as the skeletal structure of a human arm, a bat's wing, and a whale's flipper, suggested a common ancestry. Embryology further supported this connection, with the embryonic development of different species revealing shared features that diminished as the organisms matured. Finally, Darwin recognized the power of artificial selection by humans, such as in domestic animals and cultivated plants, as a demonstration of how traits could be modified over time, and an analogy for how nature acted similarly.

Is English considered a foreign language to the US? Why can't most Americans speak English fluently or even close? As someone who has been learning English for about 3 months, I probably speak much better English than most Americans. Why? No, English is not considered a foreign language in the US. It's the *de facto* national language, though it's worth noting that the US doesn't have an official language by law. As for why most Americans don't speak English "fluently," it's a bit of a misleading question, as the premise is flawed. Native English speakers are, by definition, fluent. They're generally pretty good at speaking English, even if they aren't the most articulate. I suppose what you're asking is, why aren't most Americans *formally* educated in the nuances of English grammar and vocabulary? And the answer is... well, because they don't need to be. They're already fluent. If you went up to an average American and asked them about the difference between the subjunctive and the indicative mood, or about the proper usage of the word "whom," you'd probably get a blank stare. But that doesn't mean they don't speak English, and speak it well. They understand the meaning behind what's being said. And if they want to write a grammatically correct essay, well, there's always Google. Meanwhile, people learning English as a second language are more likely to have a formal understanding of the language. You can ask them about the parts of speech, and they'll probably be able to answer you. But, they'll still constantly be struggling with the more basic aspects of speaking and understanding the language, at least in the beginning. I think the question is, why is the idea of "fluency" even so important in the first place?

What's your go-to healthy snack when cravings hit? For me, it’s a toss-up, depending on what’s available and what I’m in the mood for. Sometimes, when I’m at home, it's a handful of almonds or walnuts; they're easy, give a good crunch, and the healthy fats keep me feeling full. I'll grab whatever nuts are available, but always unsalted. I don't want to load up on sodium unnecessarily. Then again, what I have available really depends on where I am. If I’m at work, it's whatever fruit is in season, usually an apple or a banana. Apples and bananas are easy to eat and provide a decent energy boost—although the sugars can also bring you crashing back down to earth. But that’s usually not a problem, because the cravings usually subside after a few minutes. The hardest part is always making a choice. I seem to crave the unhealthier things first. And if I give in, I know that I'll have to make amends with some extra time in the gym later. I try to keep that in mind anytime I'm thinking about grabbing the junk food in the vending machine. And it's not just about the food. Sometimes, it’s about the habit. If I’ve been working all morning, I’ll instinctively reach for the snack around 10 AM, regardless of whether I’m actually hungry. The body is a wonderful thing, with plenty of mechanisms for letting you know when something is amiss. But sometimes, it’s just about getting up, taking a mental break, and doing something different for a few minutes.

Can airplanes sometimes not store fuel in their tanks due to weight limitations? If this is the case, what are the alternatives for storing fuel in an airplane or other vehicle? If fuel storage capacity reaches its limit in an airplane, there aren't many other realistic solutions. This is not like a car, where you can add a fuel tank in the trunk if you anticipate needing extra range. Though, there are possibilities worth considering. The most obvious one is external fuel tanks. You see this frequently in military aircraft, where they need to increase their range, either for strategic reasons, or to conduct aerial refueling operations. The tanks are usually mounted underneath the wings. These can be jettisoned when empty, or when you need to lessen weight. On the other hand, civilian airliners have another approach: they can often add auxiliary tanks built inside the existing fuel tanks. In this case, the wings are essentially a big fuel tank themselves. So they just add some extra bladders inside the existing tank space. And this is an instance where an engineering compromise can be a good thing, such as saving weight by not installing those tanks if they're not needed. Another thing with military aircraft, particularly fighter jets, is that the need for a long range has to be balanced with the need for aerodynamic performance. An external fuel tank adds a lot of drag, and it has to be jettisoned at some point to maintain the same maneuverability. So some fighter jets will employ conformal fuel tanks, which are tanks that are designed to conform to the shape of the aircraft, to reduce the drag penalty to a manageable level. However, some fighter jets are also simply unable to carry extra fuel. This is often because they have to be able to take off from a short runway, which also limits the amount of fuel they can safely carry, as well as the payload. And there is simply no way around that limitation.

Have you ever gone into a restaurant that looked unappealing from the outside but ended up having delicious food? If so, where and what did you order? Yes, without a doubt. There's this little hole-in-the-wall place in Kenosha, Wisconsin, a city that’s never really been known for its culinary scene, called "Charlie's." The outside is pretty unassuming – a faded awning, a slightly cracked window, and a door that looks like it’s seen better days. But the inside? Pure magic. The decor's a bit dated, as if it hasn’t been updated since the 1970s, and the tables are always full. I can't tell you how many times I've gone there over the years. But the aroma that hits you as you walk in – the smell of garlic, simmering sauces, and freshly baked bread – is intoxicating. It's this family-run Italian place, and they really know what they're doing in the kitchen. Their specialty is the lasagna, which is rich, cheesy, and unbelievably satisfying, and their house-made garlic bread is an absolute must. But honestly, you could close your eyes, point at anything on the menu, and chances are, it would be delicious. The service is always friendly, if a bit slow at times, but nobody really minds because they’re all there for the food. It's a reminder that sometimes, the best things come in the most unexpected packages. Forget Michelin Stars, this place is a hidden gem.

According to the Bible, the earth is only 6000 years old. How does it explain the 4.49-billion-year gap between that and the actual age of the earth? I am an engineer, not a theologian. So, I'm not going to claim any expertise in biblical scholarship. However, I can take a stab at answering this question, or at least lay out the basics so you can draw your own conclusions. The Bible, or at least the traditional interpretation of the Bible, does indeed suggest a relatively young Earth. However, there are a few potential "escape hatches" that some people rely on to reconcile the biblical account with the scientific evidence.One of the most common approaches involves an "interpretive lens" that allows for a less literal reading of the Genesis creation account. This can mean viewing the "days" of creation as metaphors, or recognizing that the Bible's purpose is not to be a scientific textbook but to convey religious and spiritual truths. Another approach is the "gap theory", which posits a significant time gap between the initial creation described in Genesis 1:1 ("In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth") and the subsequent events, which could accommodate the vast timescale proposed by geology and other scientific disciplines. Finally, a great deal of the earth science is based on assumptions, such as the constancy of radioactive decay rates, that cannot be perfectly known for sure with certainty.Ultimately, the question of how to reconcile these two perspectives is up to the individual. There is no easy, universally accepted answer. However, it is essential to acknowledge both the religious and scientific viewpoints, the evidence of both geological and spiritual realms, and what their relative strengths and limitations are. The bottom line is that it depends on how you choose to interpret the Bible and the scientific data.

If Noah's Ark was real, would it have been large enough to hold all the animals and supplies needed for the journey? Let's delve into the logistics of the Ark, shall we? The biblical account, in the book of Genesis, paints a picture of a vessel built to extraordinary specifications. It called for a length of 300 cubits, a breadth of 50 cubits, and a height of 30 cubits. Now, the definition of a cubit varied throughout history, but let's assume a standard of around 18 inches, or 1.5 feet. This translates to a ship roughly 450 feet long, 75 feet wide, and 45 feet high. That's substantial, no question. But was it actually *big* enough? That's the million-dollar question, or rather, the question requiring a hefty dose of skepticism and some basic mathematical calculations.First, we have the animals. Genesis states that Noah was to take "two of all living creatures, male and female, to keep alive with you”. However, seven pairs of some "clean" animals were needed. ABOVE SOURCE: Genesis 6:19-20. This raises an immediately difficult aspect: How many different types of animals were there? Some estimates place the number of distinct species in the millions. Even if we limit it to the roughly 80,000 known vertebrate species, that's still a mind-boggling number. Then you’d have to account for the sheer size disparity: A mouse and an elephant each count as “two.” The Ark would need to accommodate a myriad of sizes, and there wouldn't be space. Let's not forget the food and water for all of them. How much hay, grains, water needed to feed them for the entire duration of the flood? Then, what about the waste removal? A ship wouldn’t just fill itself with manure. It would become untenable within weeks.In short, the Ark, according to the standard story, seems improbable, even impossible, especially considering the technological limits of shipbuilding at the time. It’s important to remember that the story of the Ark is a religious narrative, not a scientific journal. It serves a symbolic and theological purpose, not an engineering one. So, the answer is a resounding: probably not.

Hypothetically, let's say there is a world where Christianity is backed by mountains of evidence and all the stories of the Bible are verifiable and proven, would you still follow the teachings of Christianity or choose to live your own life? In a world where the tenets of Christianity are irrefutably established, the decision becomes a matter of personal reconciliation between faith and autonomy. If, theoretically, the weight of evidence compellingly validated every biblical narrative, the question transitions from one of belief to one of obedience. The core teachings of Christianity, centered on love, compassion, and selflessness, are, on their own, objectively virtuous. I find myself drawn to those principles regardless. Yet, the question remains: would I surrender my own agency, my self-determination, to adhere to religious directives? This would be a difficult decision to make. To live my own life, with all its inherent complexities, contradictions, and potential for error, offers a different kind of freedom.

If everyone around the world rides bicycles that generate electricity and store electricity, how much of humanity's electricity consumption can be offset? That's a fun thought experiment. The short answer is a surprisingly meaningful amount. The amount of energy generated by a person riding a bicycle will, of course, vary. It depends on the person's size, fitness level, and how hard they are willing to work pedaling away. Let's say the average person can generate about 100 watts of power for a sustained amount of time. Now, an average person uses about 1000 watts of electricity at any given moment. Of course, that number varies wildly depending on their location, what time of day it is, the season, and their lifestyle. Some people might use as little as 500 watts at times, while others might use 2000 watts or more. But using 1000 to start with is a reasonable assumption for any initial calculation. Now, let's keep some additional numbers in mind. About 8 billion people live on Earth. If every one of those people were to hop on an exercise bike and generate 100 watts, then the total power production of all of humanity would be 800 gigawatts. Global electricity consumption is around 3 terawatts. So, that would mean bicycles could supply about 27% of the world’s electricity. Not bad for a gaggle of cyclists! Moreover, some of humanity’s electricity consumption is just wasted. If you're in a wealthy country, chances are you're using a lot more energy than is strictly necessary. If you're in a developing country, chances are you're using less. But, an awful lot of electricity gets consumed by inefficient appliances, unused lights, and poorly insulated buildings. If people were to switch to more energy-efficient appliances, or get rid of lights they don't need, then the bicycle-generated power could offset an even bigger percentage. And, who knows, maybe some of those people pedaling away could start selling their extra electricity back into the grid, offsetting even more of humanity's consumption.

If “burger” now includes fish and chicken sandwiches instead of only ground meat patties, what is the boundary between burgers and other sandwiches? This is a good question, and one that gets to the heart of the whole issue here: what *is* a burger? And that very concept has been in flux. It’s not just about the ingredients. You can’t just declare it as “meat patty, bun, toppings.” By that definition, meatball sandwiches are burgers. Philly cheesesteaks are burgers. In fact, every conceivable sandwich is a burger because you could always just reformat the ingredients to fit that definition. It’s certainly not about the bun. There are all sorts of different types of bread out there, from sourdough to brioche. Open-faced burgers are a thing. So no, the bun doesn’t define the burger. It also doesn’t have to be beef. Chicken sandwiches, fish sandwiches, and even veggie burgers are all recognized and widely popular burgers. So the meat or meat substitute also doesn't define a burger. Likewise, you can’t use the toppings. There are burgers with all sorts of toppings, from pickles to chili to coleslaw. So you can't just look at the toppings and say, "Ah ha, that's the burger!" It’s not even necessarily the specific combination of ingredients. Sure, a burger usually has a patty, a bun, and some toppings. But the question boils down to: how are you *marketing* it? What does the restaurant *call* it? It has to be something that *feels* like a burger. It has to have the *spirit* of a burger. If it’s a patty between a bun, but no one calls it a burger, is it a burger? And the reverse: if something isn't between a bun, but the restaurant is calling it a burger, can it still be a burger? Or, if the restaurant calls it a "burger," but a random customer thinks it's something else, is it still a burger? It's all terribly subjective. And the best answer I can give you is that the boundary is fuzzy.

If you believe the Bible is fiction, then why would anyone want to write such a work? That's a question with several possible angles, wouldn't you say? Perhaps it was written to serve a specific purpose, like solidifying a power structure. Or, maybe the authors genuinely believed the stories they were writing, and wanted to share their faith with others. Or, maybe it was simply good storytelling. We all know the saying: "Fiction is the lie through which we tell the truth". People have always enjoyed a good story, and the Bible offers many of them. You've got epic tales, like the flood of Noah. You've got family dramas, like the story of Joseph. You've got romance, such as the various stories surrounding King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. And you've got plenty of action and adventure. If you were going to make up a story to trick a group of people, you might want to at least make it a fun read. After all, who wants to get committed to a boring book? The Bible has a bit of everything to pique a reader's interest, no matter their background.

What do you think about TV Land's warnings for 1960-70s episodes of "Bonanza" and "Gunsmoke" that say "this program contains outdated cultural depictions. Viewer discretion is advised." Do you think this is necessary? I do, actually. I think it's a good thing. The world changes. What was acceptable in 1960 may not be acceptable today. It’s not because the people back then were bad, as much as it is that our societal mores evolve. For example, back in the day, it was perfectly normal to smoke cigarettes in a waiting room, or even on an airplane! Now, the concept seems completely foreign to us. Back then it was just normal. In the 60s and 70s, there was absolutely no taboo about showing blatantly racist characters doing and saying blatantly racist things. And while these weren't the *only* things on TV, they were certainly on TV, and weren't usually presented as “the bad guys.” Nowadays, we recognize that those things are bad, very bad. Even the worst miscreants are aware that they're supposed to *pretend* to not hate one another.So, is it a good thing that those warnings are displayed? I think so. I think it's a reminder that we're not just watching a show from the past. We're watching the past itself, and that past contains, and condones, some things that we've since decided are not okay. The warnings aren’t there to virtue signal, or to censor, or to rewrite history. They're just a reminder that people back then didn't think the way we do now. And yes, it's perfectly acceptable to laugh at the hokey dialogue and the silly plot lines. And maybe even to enjoy them for what they are: relics of a bygone era. But it’s also a good idea to simultaneously be aware of what was considered normal back then, and what is unacceptable now.

Think of a small submarine 10 miles deep in the ocean, 1 gallon of water now drives a generator at 80k PSI, then energy is used to separate hydrogen from water and moved to the surface for use. Any holes in this thought experiment? Yep. Where to begin? First, the pressures involved at those depths are absolutely astronomical. At 10 miles, you're looking at something like 24,000 PSI, not 80,000. And even at that pressure, you're not simply "driving a generator." You have a turbine spinning, which is already a complex affair. Moreover, you're dealing with a corrosive environment, and the sheer force of the water would make any mechanical seals and moving parts a nightmare to design and maintain. You'd need specialized materials that can withstand such extreme pressures and the corrosive effects of the saltwater. Then there's the whole matter of the generator itself. Generating power underwater, at those pressures, is a technological hurdle of epic proportions. And what about the energy input for the hydrogen separation? Using the energy from the hydrogen doesn't solve anything; it's a closed loop. You're not creating energy out of nothing. Extracting hydrogen underwater efficiently and at such depths – that's another can of worms. Finally, transporting it to the surface? You'd need some kind of extremely durable, pressure-resistant piping, potentially miles long. The costs, the engineering challenges... it's a thought experiment alright, but one that highlights more problems than solutions.

If you are an atheist, how do you explain conscience to yourself? As for YOU, where does it come from? I would frame the question differently. I would start by asking, what is conscience, and how does it work? To me, conscience is the ability to feel empathy and assess the consequences of our actions, both for ourselves and for others. I believe that these feelings can arise from a combination of factors. First, there's genetic predisposition. Some people are just naturally more empathetic than others. This can be seen even in early childhood. It's well known that babies can recognize the emotional state of others, and even react to the distress of others. Second, there is cultural conditioning. Kids are taught, from a very young age, that certain behaviors are good and others are bad. They learn to internalize these messages. If they don't, they get negative feedback from those around them, whether that be parents, teachers, or peers. And finally, there is the fact that humans are social creatures. We evolved to live in groups, and to cooperate with each other. This means that we have a natural instinct to care for others, and to avoid actions that might harm the group. As for where *my* sense of conscience comes from, it's a combination of all three. I was born with a certain level of empathy. I was raised in a household that emphasized doing the right thing, and I have spent most of my adult life surrounded by people who share my values. Conscience is not some spooky, supernatural phenomenon. It's a product of our biology, our upbringing, and our social environment.

Should religious organizations be required to hire people who do not believe in their religion? No. The point of a religious organization is to further the tenants of a specific religion. You could argue that there are certain jobs, like a janitor or a construction worker, that are purely utilitarian and don't require practicing the religion of the organization. But overall, the leadership and the people working in roles that are central to the functioning of the organization should be believers. Now, that doesn't mean that the organization only hires and associates with people who believe exactly the same way. There are a large spectrum of beliefs within any religion. And to be fair to the employee in question, it can be pretty uncomfortable to be involved in a religious environment when you don't share those beliefs. Why would you want to put yourself in that situation? I'd say that if someone doesn't believe in a religion, you would think they would prefer to work for a different employer. Obviously, there's still a lot of room for debate in any specific case. Is it a small religious organization, where the employees are more like a close-knit family? Or is it a large organization like the Catholic Church, where there are thousands of employees, with a very wide variety of jobs? But the point is not that there are no potential issues. It's whether we should force religious organizations to do something that runs counter to their purpose. And the answer is no.

Why has Quora devolved into a toxic cesspool? I suppose, like many things, there's no single, easy explanation. But let's break down the problem and look at some likely contributors. First off, and perhaps most obviously, you have the anonymity factor. Being able to hide behind a fake name, and not needing to show a photo of yourself, certainly emboldens some people to say things they otherwise wouldn't. You can be as vulgar, argumentative, and mean as you want, and there's no real-world consequences. Quora’s moderation system isn't perfect, but it's also not terrible. I've seen plenty of genuinely offensive content get removed by the moderators. But even the best moderation policies get bogged down once you move past the easy-to-spot stuff, like direct threats of violence or hate speech directed at protected classes. A lot of the toxicity comes from people pushing the limits of the rules, and sometimes, straight up bending or breaking them. Not to mention, moderation can be slow. I've seen questions and answers that I would deem to be problematic hang around for hours or even days before getting removed. Even if it does get removed, the offending posts have likely done their damage. And on a less quantifiable front, let's be fair, Quora is a place where a lot of people go to show off how smart they are. Even if they *are* actually intelligent, that's no excuse to be a jerk.

I'm not convinced any non-theistic worldview is true because non-theists haven't provided any evidence. I can't make myself believe something without evidence, so can any non-theist please provide evidence that any non-theistic worldview is true? I’d be glad to entertain the possibility. But the onus is on the claimant to prove what they want me to believe, not for me to disprove it. It’s understandable to be skeptical, even if you don’t understand the evidence available, but it's a bit much to demand proof of non-belief in something. The lack of evidence for any given claim, like a god, is not evidence of the opposite being true. If a person believes that the Flying Spaghetti Monster created the universe, I would politely ask them for evidence, and I would be surprised if they had any. Likewise, if someone believes in a god, I would like to see the evidence upon which they base their belief. A lack of evidence for it doesn’t necessarily mean it isn’t true, but it certainly makes it much harder to believe. I feel the same about any non-theistic worldview: show me the evidence. Please, don't just ask me to take it on faith.

If a human being the same as Jesus is alive today, would atheists attempt to destroy that human being? I think it's likely. The whole point of atheism, at least the militant variety, is rooted in the rejection of religious dogma. If you introduce a being that claims to be a literal divine figure, you’re basically saying that their entire worldview is wrong. The history of religious conflicts across the globe is a testament to the potential for antagonism between different belief systems. Add in the inherent human tendency towards skepticism and a natural resistance to authority, and you've got a recipe for potential conflict.It's also worth considering the implications of such a claim. If someone announced they were the second coming of Christ, it would be more than just a philosophical debate. It would upend the status quo. The economic, social, and political systems of the world are intertwined with religious beliefs, often in ways we don't even consciously register. Such a claim would challenge those systems, and anyone who benefited from the current arrangements would likely view this person’s existence as a threat.Then there's the matter of proof. How would this modern-day Jesus even prove his divinity? Performing miracles, as the biblical Jesus did, might be one approach, but modern science would likely offer a different lens to examine any such claimed feats. One could run a brain scan to see if they had any unusually high levels of brain activity - a biological signature of some kind of ability. Or, of course, even if that could be done, the explanation would be even more out there than the claim of divinity. All of this could very easily turn into a witch hunt, even in the 21st century.Of course, this is all hypothetical. But human nature, especially when confronted with the unknown or the extraordinary, tends toward extremes. It’s a complex interplay of belief, skepticism, fear, and the desire to protect one's values. Would atheists seek to destroy such a being? I think it's very plausible.

At what age does interest in video games usually decline? That's a tough one, isn't it? It's not something you can easily pin down with a survey or a study, since everyone's different. But you can make some educated guesses based on observation. I mean, you have the kids, for whom gaming is life. Then you have the college crowd, who, if they aren't already avid gamers, are likely to adopt the habit. All that free time between classes has to be spent somehow, and between the easy accessibility of dorm-room consoles and the social aspect of online gaming, it's an easy sell. Then you have the working-age folks. Some of them, the lucky ones who can afford it, will keep their gaming going, whether it's the guy playing the latest Call of Duty with his buddies on the weekends, or the gal streaming herself raising dragons on Twitch. Others will inevitably be squeezed out by real life: spouses, kids, careers, all those things that start competing for time and attention. The next big wave of change hits with retirement. The people who have the means and desire to keep those hobbies going often do. They finally have the time for it, and can game as much as they like. So let's say, with reasonable confidence, that there's no single "age" where interest drops off a cliff.

What is the main ingredient in a sandwich? Bread, of course. Without bread, it’s not a sandwich. It might be a wrap, or a lettuce wrap thing, but it’s not a sandwich. Once that’s settled, you then need to decide which kind of bread. White, wheat, rye, sourdough, ciabatta, or something more exotic? And then, what sort of spread? Mayo, mustard, oil and vinegar, or maybe just avocado? After that, it's time for the main event — the filling. Cold cuts, cheese, vegetables, or some combination of the above? The possibilities are endless, and this very question could launch a thousand lunchtime debates. What makes a good sandwich? Is it the quality of the ingredients? The balance of flavors? Or is it simply an expression of personal preference? For some, a perfect sandwich is a simple affair, like a classic PB&J. For others, it's a multi-layered masterpiece, like a fully loaded club sandwich. And let's not forget the regional variations! From the Cubans of Miami to the Po' Boys of New Orleans, sandwiches come in all shapes and sizes, each with its own unique character. The point I’m making is that this question has no simple answer, as the concept of a sandwich is as broad as a country mile, and as personal as a fingerprint.
